title: Support vectors & the margin
intro: The secret of SVMs: the majority of your training data can be thrown away without the model changing. The few examples that do matter are called support vectors — and they also explain why kernel SVMs are so fast.

blocks.html:
Continuing from chapter 3: logistic regression is a linear classifier, learned with the logistic loss. A linear SVM is also a linear classifier, but with the hinge loss — and the standard definition of an SVM adds L2 regularisation to that by default. The loss diagrams of chapter 2 therefore look strikingly similar.

The crucial difference is the flat section of the hinge loss: as soon as the raw model output exceeds +1 — you predicted the example correctly, with a certain error margin — the loss is exactly zero. When a training example falls in that "zero-loss zone", it contributes nothing to the fit: remove the example and the model does not change. This is the defining feature of SVMs.

blocks.label: SVM = hinge + L2
blocks.caption: The standard SVM: hinge loss per example plus L2 regularisation on the coefficients.

sections.title: Support vectors: the examples that matter

blocks.html:
Support vectors are the examples that do not fall in the flat section — in formula form: examples with \( y_i \, f(x_i) \le 1 \). These are (1) the incorrectly classified examples and (2) the correctly classified examples close to the boundary. How close is "close enough" is steered by the regularisation strength.

Compare that with logistic regression: there is no flat section there — every data point influences the fit. With an SVM it is precisely the non-support vectors that are remarkable: you can throw them away without any effect. Critical for the popularity of SVMs: kernel SVMs (later in this chapter) are surprisingly fast, partly because clever algorithms scale only with the number of support vectors instead of the total number of training examples.

blocks.caption: How much of your data is actually a support vector?
blocks.source:
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine

X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)

svc = SVC(kernel='linear', C=1.0).fit(X, y)

print('Training examples  :', len(X))
print('Support vectors    :', len(svc.support_vectors_))
print('Per class          :', svc.n_support_)
print('Training score     :', round(svc.score(X, y), 3))

blocks.html: Remove a non-support vector → the model does not change. Remove a support vector → the model does change. Support vectors are literally the examples that "carry" the model.

Outside this course you will often see SVMs described as "margin maximizers" — for completeness, that picture. On a linearly separable dataset the learned boundary falls exactly halfway between the two classes. That is attractive: without extra information, a boundary that gives both classes equal room is more sensible than one pressed tightly against a single class.

The distance from the support vectors to the boundary is called the margin. As long as the regularisation strength is not too large, the SVM maximises the margin on separable data. Most datasets, however, are not linearly separable (don't expect 100% training accuracy), but the max-margin idea turned out to be mathematically equivalent to what we already had: hinge loss + L2 regularisation. Two pairs of glasses, the same model.

blocks.label: margin
blocks.caption: The width of the buffer zone around the decision boundary. Maximising the margin = minimising ‖w‖ — hence the L2 penalty.

blocks.html: Why does this work exactly? The hinge loss demands correct predictions with a margin (\( y\,f(x) \ge 1 \)); the L2 term keeps \( \lVert w \rVert \) small — and together that pushes the boundary exactly into the middle.
